la:verb:stimulo.gloss: to urge on, goad on, stimulate, rouse up
senses: to urge on, goad on, stimulate, rouse up
to torment, vex, trouble, disquiet, disturb
la:verb:stimulo.html:
stĭmŭlo, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a.
id.
,
to prick with a goad, to prick or goad on, to urge on (syn. pungo).
Lit. (post-Aug. and rare): quadrijugos flagello,: equos calcaribus,; for which, poet. transf.: turbatos currus,; : aries stimulatus,.—
Trop., to goad, torment, vex, trouble, disquiet, disturb (class. and freq.; syn. agito): jactor, crucior, agitor, stimulor, vorsor in amoris rota miser,: hunc sibi ex animo scrupulum, qui se dies noctesque stimulat ac pungit, ut evellatis, postulat,: larvae stimulant virum,: te conscientiae stimulant maleficiorum tuorum,: me nunc et congressus hujus (Caesaris) stimulat,: me haec solitudo minus stimulat quam ista celebritas,: consulem cura de minore filio stimulabat,: stimulatus furenti rabie,: curis animum stimulantibus,.—
In gen., to rouse up, set in motion; to spur on, incite, stimulate to any action (syn. cieo, excio).
With simple acc.: Phrygio stimulat numero cava tibia mentes,: aliquem,: avita gloria animum stimulabat,: irā stimulante animos,; : cupido animum stimulabat,; : stimulata pellicis irā,.—With inanim. objects: jurgia praecipue vino stimulata,: Persicorum sucus sitim stimulat,; so, venerem,; cf. conceptus,: fugam hostium,: iras functas,to revive, arouse,. —
With ad: ad alicujus salutem defendendam stimulari atque excitari,: ad perturbandam rempublicam,: ad arma,: ad iram,.—
With in: injuriae dolor in Tarquinium eos stimulabat,: animos eorum irā in hostes stimulando,; cf. in a mixed construction: ad iram saepius quam in formidinem stimulabantur,—
With ut or ne: vetus nostra simultas antea stimulabat me, ut caverem, etc.,: rubore stimulabantur, ne clientulorum loco numerarentur,; .—(ε) Poet., with inf.: festinare fugam ... iterum stimulat,: stimulante metu fati praenoscere cursus,: juvencos jactare accensis stimulavi cornibus ignes,.—(ζ) Absol.: stimulante fame,: stimulante conscientiā,: metu stimulante,.

la:noun:stipulatio.html:
stĭpŭlātĭo, ōnis, f.
stipulor
, jurid. t. t.,
a promise given on demand; an engagement, agreement, bargain, covenant, stipulation, obligation (syn. pactum), : stipulatio est verborum conceptio, quibus is qui interrogatur, daturum facturumve se, quod interrogatus est, respondet,: stipulatio non potest confici, nisi utroque loquente, etc.,: pacta, conventa, stipulationes,: ut ea pecunia ex stipulatione debeatur,: aliquem stipulatione alligare,: nondum stipulationes legeram,: stipulationum et judiciorum formulas conponere,; ; pr.; : is contractus stipulationum sponsionum sponsalia, Serv. Suip. ap. ; .

la:noun:stipendium.html:
stīpendĭum, ii, n.
contr. from stipipendium, from stips-pendo
.
In publicists' lang., a tax, impost, tribute, contribution (payable in money; whereas vectigal in kind; the former being regarded as the more humiliating; v. stipendiarius, I.): Poeni stipendia pendunt, Enn. ap. Müll. (Ann. v. 269 Vahl.); so, pendere,; ; ; ; : conferre,: solvere,: imponere victis,; : stipendio liberare aliquem,: de stipendio recusare,: stipendi spem facere,.—
Transf.
In gen., tribute, dues (poet. and in post-Aug. prose): indomito nec dira ferens stipendia tauro (sc. Minotauro),: quae finis aut quod me manet stipendium?penalty,: alii tamen obscuriores (scriptores) aliquod stipendium nostro studio contulerunt,contribution,.—
Income, subsistence, salary: iis, ut adsiduae templi antistites essent, stipendium de publico statuit,.—
In milit. lang., pay, stipend in full: stipendium militare,; ; commonly stipendium alone: militis stipendia ideo, quod eam stipem pendebant, Müll.; cf. ; and 60: cum stipendium ab legionibus flagitaretur,: numerare militibus,: persolvere,: dare, Brut. ap. ; ; ; cf.: dare pecuniam in stipendium,; : accipere,: stipendio afficere exercitum,: augere,: fraudare,: stipendium duum mensium,: dum in calamitosis stipendiis versaretur,might get pay by the misfortunes of others,.—
Transf., military service (mostly in plur.): merere stipendia,: stipendia merere (mereri),to perform military service, to serve,; ; also, facere,; ; ; ; cf.: opulenta ac ditia facere,: emereri,to complete the time of service, to serve out one's time,; Cic. Sen. 14, 49; ; ; ; v. emereo, II.: auxiliaria stipendia mereri,: numerare,: enumerare,: qui (milites) jam stipendiis confecti erant,; cf.: stipendiis exhausti,: adulescentuli statim castrensibus stipendiis imbuebantur,.— Sing.: homo nullius stipendii,: exercitui dare, Dietsch: sextus decimus stipendii annus,.—
In partic., military service of a year, a year's service, a campaign: si in singulis stipendiis is ad hostes exuvias dabit,: quod tricena aut quadragena stipendia senes tolerent,: vicena stipendia meritis,: stipendia sua numerari jubebant,: qui eorum minime multa stipendia haberet,fin.—Sing.: (juventus) octavo jam stipendio functa,; cf. with both numbers together: secundo stipendio dextram manum perdidit, stipendiis duobus ter et vicies vulneratus est, § 104.—
Trop., in gen., service (very rare): functus omnibus humanae vitae stipendiis,i. e. duties,: tamquam emeritis stipendiis libidinis,: plurium velut emeritis annorum stipendiis,: rex cui (Hercules) duodecim stipendia debebat,services, labors,.

la:noun:stimulus.html:
stĭmŭlus, i, m.
for stig-mulus, from the root stig; Gr. στίζω; v. stilus
.
A goad for driving cattle, slaves, etc. (class.,

esp. in the trop. sense).

Lit.: jam lora teneo, jam stimulum in manu: Agite equi, etc.,: parce, puer, stimulis, et fortius utere loris,: aut stimulo tardos increpuisse boves, (12); cf. : ita te forabunt patibulatum per vias Stimulis,: aliquem stimulo fodere,: dum te stimulis fodiam,: numquam stimulo lacessat juvencum,.—As a term of abuse of slaves: stimulorum seges,; cf. : stimulorum tritor,.—Prov.: si stimulos pugnis caedis, manibus plus dolet,i. e. an evil is aggravated by foolish opposition,; cf.: advorsum stimulum calces,kick against the pricks,.—
Trop., a goad (as in Engl., either that which vexes, irritates, torments, or, more freq., that which spurs on, incites, stimulates).
A sting, torment, pang: mens sibi conscia factis ... adhibet stimulos torretque flagellis,; cf.: subesse caecum aliquem cordi stimulum,: ne illa stimulum longum habet, quae usque illinc cor pungit meum,: stimulos doloris contemnere,; cf.: (res malae) lacerant, vexant, stimulos admovent, etc.,: stimulos in pectore caecos Condidit,.—
A spur, incentive, incitement, stimulus: animum gloriae stimulis concitare,: quidam industriae ac laboris (with illecebrae libidinum),: quot stimulos admoverit homini victoriae studioso,; cf.: defendendi Vatinii,: omnia pro stimulis facibusque ciboque furoris Accipit,: ardet, et injusti stimulis agitatur amoris,: non hostili modo odio sed amoris etiam stimulis,: ad hanc voluntatem ipsius naturae stimulis incitamur,: ad dicendum etiam pudor stimulos habet,: agrariae legis tribuniciis stimulis plebs furebat,; cf.: acriores quippe aeris alieni stimulos esse,: subdere stimulos animo,: in aliquem stimulis accendi,; cf.: suis stimulis excitos Moesiae duces,: secundae res acrioribus stimulis animos explorant,: acres Subjectat lasso stimulos,: stimulos sub pectore vertit Apollo,: movere acres stimulos irarum,: accensae stimulis majoribus irae,: dare stimulos laudum,.—
In milit. lang., a pointed stake concealed beneath the surface of the ground, to repel hostile troops (syn.: sudes, stipes),: se stimulis induere,.

la:verb:stipo.gloss: to crowd or press together, compress
senses: to crowd or press together, compress
la:verb:stipo.html:
stīpo, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a.
στέφω, to surround, crowd upon, στέμμα, στέφανος; cf.: stipator, stipulor
,
to crowd or press together, to compress (class.; esp. of personal objects, and in part. perf.; cf.: comprimo, compono).
Lit.: qui acceperant majorem numerum (assium), non in arcā ponebant, sed in aliquā cellā stipabant, id est componebant, quo minus loci occuparet, Müll.: ingens argentum,: apes mella Stipant,; : materies stipata,: nec tamen undique corporea stipata tenentur omnia naturā,; cf. ; ; : Graeci stipati, quini in lectulis, saepe plures,: velut stipata phalanx,: ita in arto stipatae erant naves, ut, etc.,: fratrum stipata cohors,.— Poet.: stipare Platona Menandro, i. e. to pack up together the works of Plato, Menander, etc., : custodum gregibus circa seu stipat euntem,closely surrounds her with, (4, 7), 13; cf. mid.: cuncta praecipiti stipantur saecula cursu,throng, crowd,.—
Transf., to press, cram, stuff, or fill full of any thing: ut pontes calonibus et impedimentis stipatos reperit,: hos (poëtas) ediscit et hos arcto stipata theatro Spectat Roma,; cf.: curia cum patribus fuerit stipata,: multo Patrum stipatur curia coetu,: recessus equi,: tribunal,: calathos prunis,: nucein sulfure,: calceum,: tectum omne,.—
With a personal object, of a dense crowd, to surround, encompass, environ, attend, accompany,

etc. (syn.: comitor, prosequor): Catilina stipatus choro juventutis, vallatus indicibus atque sicariis,: qui stipatus semper sicariis, saeptus armatis, munitus indicibus fuit,: stipati gregibus amicorum,; cf. : telis stipati,: qui senatum stiparit armatis,: stipatus lictoribus,: senectus stipata studiis juventutis,: comitum turba est stipata suarum,: juventus stipat ducem,; ; et Balb. 13.—Absol.: magnă stipante catervă,; : huc coetus ministrūm stipantur,. —Hence, * stīpātus, a, um, P. a., begirt, surrounded: ab omni ordine, sexu, aetate stipatissimus,.

la:noun:stirpes.gloss: rootstock; the lowest part of the trunk of a plant, including the roots.

la:noun:stirps.gloss: rootstock; the lowest part of the trunk of a plant, including the roots.
senses: rootstock; the lowest part of the trunk of a plant, including the roots.
la:noun:stirps.html:
stirps (collat. form of the nom.stir-pes or stirpis, in the best MSS., ; ; ; v. Drak. ad locc.), pis, f. (poet. and post-Aug.; also m., Enn. ap. Müll., and ap. (Ann. 184); Pac. ap. (Trag. Fragm. 421), and ap. P.; ; ; ; ; ; ; ; cf. ) [root star-; cf. sternere; Gr. στορέννυμι; prop. that which extends or spreads].
Lit., the lower part of the trunk of plants, including the roots; a stock, stem, stalk; a root (class. and very freq.; cf. radix): arborum altitudo nos delectat. radices stirpesque non item,: terra stirpes amplexa alat,; cf. ; 2, 47, 120; 2, 51, 127: ut tantum modo per stirpis alantur suas,: sceptrum in silvis imo de stirpe recisum,: harundo omnis ex unā stirpe numerosa, Plin. 16, 36, 65, § 163: palmarum stirpibus ali,; so, palmarum,, § 131 (for which: radices palmarum,, § 87); cf.: lento in stirpe moratus, (for which, just before: lentā in radice): stirpes raptas volvere,: validis amplexae stirpibus ulmos,: hic stirpes obruit arvo,: domos avium cum stirpibus imis Eruit,; cf. of hair: vellere albos ab stirpe capillos, : ex hac nimiā licentiā, ut ex stirpe quādam, exsistere, etc.,.—
Transf.
Of vegetables.
A plant, shrub (esp. freq. in plur.): stirpium naturae,; cf.: cum arborum et stirpium eadem paene natura sit,; so (with arbores) ; (with herbae) : pati (terram) stirpium asperitate vastari,: stirpes tenent,: internatas saxis stirpes et herbas vellentes,.—
A shoot, sprout: rami stirpesque,: stirpem praecisum circumligato, etc.,: probatissimum genus stirpis deponere, i. e. malleolos,: stirpem post annum praecidi,: stirpis committere ramis,engraft,.—
Of persons.
A stem, stock, race, family, lineage (cf.: genus, familia): ignoratio stirpis et generis,: stirpis ac gentilitatis jus,: qui sunt ejusdem stirpis,: a stirpe supremo, Enn. ap. (Ann. v. 184 Vahl.): divinae stirpis Acestes,: Priami de stirpe,: Herculis stirpe generatus,: hinc orti stirpe antiquissimā sumus,: hominum sceleratorum,: ab stirpe socius et amicus populi Romani, et saep.: unum relictum, stirpem genti Fabiae futurum,—
Like Engl. scion, = offspring, descendant, progeny (mostly poet.; not in Cic.): stirps liberum, Enn. ap. Müll. (Trag. v. 317 Vahl.); so, liberum,; cf.: aliquis magnā de stirpe nepotum,: stirps et genus omne futurum,; cf.: en stirps et progenies tot consulum, tot dictatorum,: stirpis virilis,; cf.: qui stirpem ex sese domi relinquerent,.—
Trop., source, origin, foundation, first beginning, cause, etc.: altae stirpes stultitiae,: superstitionis stirpes,: virtutis,: quā ex stirpe orirentur amicitiae cognationum,: quodsi exquiratur usque ab stirpe auctoritas,: populum a stirpe repetere, Mos.: repetam stirpem juris a naturā,: stirps ac semen malorum omnium,; cf.: ea pars, quae quasi stirps est hujus quaestionis,: non ingenerantur hominibus mores tam a stirpe generis ac seminis, quam, etc.,original nature,; cf.: exoletā stirpe gentis,.—So esp. in phrase ab stirpe, utterly: Karthago ab stirpe interiit,: gens ab stirpe exstincta est,: omne genus ab stirpe sublatum esse,; cf.: omnis intra annum cum stirpe exstinctos,: velut ab stirpibus renata urbs,.

la:noun:stirpis.gloss: rootstock; the lowest part of the trunk of a plant, including the roots.
senses: alternative form of stirps (“rootstock; sprout; offspring”)

la:noun:stipes.html:
stīpĕs, ĭtis (collat. form stips, stīpis, ), m.
root stip-, = Gr. στεφ-; v. stipo; Sanscr. sthapa-jami, to cause to stand, to fix, place; cf. stipula
.
Lit., a log, stock, post, trunk of a tree, etc. (class.; syn.: palus, sudes),; ; ; (21); ; ; ; ; ; ; : deligare ad stipitem,to a stake,.—As a term of contempt, like our log, stock, post, of a stupid person: in me quidvis harum rerum convenit, Quae sunt dicta in stultum, caudex, stipes, asinus, plumbeus,: qui, tamquam truncus atque stipes, si stetisset modo, posset sustinere tamen titulum consulatus,; cf. ; id. ap. Senat. 6, 14; .—
Transf., poet.
A tree, ; id. de Nuce, 32; ; Claud. Cons. Prob. et Olybr. 179.—
A branch of a tree, ; : candelabri, the main stem of the candlestick, .

la:noun:stipula.html:
stĭpŭla, ae, f.dim.
stipes
,
a stalk, stem, blade, halm; of grain (syn. culmus): frumenta in viridi stipulā lactentia turgent,; ; ; : e segete ad spicilegium stipulam relinquere, Müll.—Of the stalks of grain left behind in reaping, straw, stubble, ; ; ; ; : in stipulā placidi carpebat munera somni,; cf. .—Of hay, .—Of a reed, ; .—Of bean-stalks, . —Prov.: flammaque de stipulā nostra brevisque fuit,of a quickly extinguished fire,: postmodo de stipulā magnus acervus erit,.

la:adj:stipulus.html:
stĭpŭlus, a, um, adj. (old Lat.),
firm: stipulum apud veteres firmum appellabatur,; .

senses: a stylus or pencil used for writing on waxen tablets
la:noun:stilus.html:
stĭlus (not stylus), i, m.
for stiglus; Gr. στίζω, to stick, puncture; στίγμα, mark, point; Sanscr. tig, to be sharp; tigmas, sharp; cf. Engl. stick, sting; Lat. stimulus; not connected with στῦλος
.
In gen., a stake, pale: extra vallum stili caeci, concealed stakes, Auct. B. Afr. 31, 5; cf. (for which stimuli, ): ligneus,; .—In agriculture, a pointed instrument for freeing plants from worms or from shoots which grow too rankly, etc., ; .—Of the stem or stalk of many plants (e. g. of the asparagus), ; ; ; 5, 10, 21.—
In partic.
A style used by the Romans for writing on waxen tablets (pointed, and usually made of iron): effer cito stilum, ceram et tabellas et linum,; cf. ; 4, 9, 73; : cum otiosus stilum prehenderat, flaccebat oratio,: orationes paene Attico stilo scriptae,with an Attic pen,; so, (comoediae quaedam) resipiant stilum Plautinum,.—And with reference to the ecenomical use, in a double sense, .—Writing on wax was erased with the broad upper end of the style; hence the phrase stilum vertere, for to erase what one has written, : saepe stilum vertas, iterum quae digna legi sint, Scripturus,.—But cf.: et mihi vertenti stilum in Gallias,i. e. turning to write of,.—Comically: stilis me totum usque ulmeis conscribito,i. e. with elm switches, (cf. conscribo).—
Transf.
= scriptio and scriptura, a setting down in writing, composing, composition; the practice of composing; manner of writing, mode of composition: stilus optimus et praestantissimus dicendi effector ac magister,; ; cf. ; ; cf.: multus stilus et assidua lectio,: stilus exercitatus,i. e. a practised pen,: tardior stilus cogitationem moratur,: neglegens,: multus,: tardus,: rudis et confusus,: fidelis,: stilo incumbere,: aliquid stilo prosequi,; 2, 3, 3: signare stilo,: non ita dissimili sunt argumento, sed tamen Dissimili oratione sunt factae ac stilo,in speech and writing, (for which: oratione et scripturā,); cf.: unus sonus est totius orationis et idem stilus,the same tone and the same style of composition run through the whole speech,: artifex stilus,an artistic style,: familiares opes velut supremo distribuens stilo,i. e. by his last will,.—
A manner of speaking, mode of expression, style in speaking (post-Aug. and very rare; not as early as Quint.; in class. Lat. sermo, oratio, dictio, dicendi modus, ars, genus or forma): stilus pressus demissusque,, 5: pugnax et quasi bellatorins,: laetior,; cf.: diligentis stili anxietas,: (Octavius) tragoediam magno impetu exorsus, non succedente stilo, abolevit,: affectatione obscurabat stilum,: stili dicendi duo sunt: unus est maturus et gravis, alter ardens erectus et infensus, etc.,; .—*
A decision, verdict, opinion, .

stilus, I.

la:other:Stimula.html:
Stĭmŭla (Sĭmĭla, ), ae, f.
stimulus
,
the goddess who pricks on, excites, stimulates to action or pleasure, Aug. Civ Del, 4, 11; 4, 16; perh. for Semele,; Schol. ; cf. Müller, Etrusk. 2, 77.

la:noun:stips.html:
stips, stĭpis (nom. does not occur, although stips is assumed by Müll.; P.; cf. Gloss. stips, ἔρανος), f.
kindr. with stipo, and therefore, orig., small coin in heaps; hence, in partic.
,
a gift, donation, alms, contribution, given in small coin: etiam nunc dis cum thesauris asses dant, stipem dicunt, Müll.: stipem esse nummum signatum testimonio est, quod datur in stipendium militi et cum spondetur pecunia, quod stipulari dicitur, Fest. pp. 296 and 297 Müll.; cf.: stipendium a stipe appellatum est, quod per stipes, id est modica aera colligatur,: stipem Apollini conferre,; so of religious donations, ; ; ; ; : quis beneficium dicat quadram panis aut stipem aeris abjecti,; so of alms, ; ; cf. ; : ad captandas stipes,; : pastiones non minimam colono stipem conferunt,bring in no small profit,: suburbanum hortum exiguā colere stipe,: parvā cur stipe quaerat opes,; cf. : e prostitutis ancilla mercenariae stipis,living by the wages of prostitution,: nodosam exsolvite stipem,penalty,.

la:noun:stilla.gloss: a drop of a dense, viscous liquid or other non-natural substance (e.g., oil, sap; vinegar)
senses: a drop of a dense, viscous liquid or other non-natural substance (e.g., oil, sap; vinegar)
la:noun:stilla.html:
stilla, ae, f.
dim. of stĭria; cf. Fest. s. v. stiricipium, p. 345 Müll.; Corss. 1, p. 518
,
a drop (a dense, viscous, gummy, fatty drop; whereas gutta is a natural, liquid drop: gutta imbrium est, stilla olei vel aceti, Roth).
Lit. (rare but class.): stilla muriae, * ; : sicca et sine stillis arbor,; : olei,: stilla saeva (arborum),.—
Transf., a drop, i. e. a small quantity (post-Aug.): olei,.—Trop.: pauculae temporum,a very little, a moment.—
In later Lat. = gutta, stillae pluviae, : roris,: pluviarum,.

la:noun:stillicidium.gloss: liquid (especially rainwater) falling drop by drop
senses: liquid (especially rainwater) falling drop by drop
la:noun:stillicidium.html:
stillĭcĭdĭum (also written stilĭcĭd-; v. Lachm. ad ), ii, n.
stilla-cado
,
a liquid which falls drop by drop, a dripping moisture, stillicide: stillicidium eo quod stillatim cadat, Müll.
In gen. (poet. and in post-Aug. prose): stillicidi casus lapidem cavat,: grandinis,: urinae,; cf. vesicae,: arborum,: mellis,: raritas nubium stillicidia dispergit, App. de Mundo, p. 61.—
Trop.: per stillicidia emittere animam quam semel exhalare,little by little,.—
In partic., falling rain, rain-water falling from the eaves of houses (class.): jura parietum, luminum, stillicidiorum,; ; ; ; ; ; .

la:adj:stipendiarius.html:
stĭ_pendĭārĭus, a, um, adj.
id.
.
Of or belonging to tribute, liable to impost or contribution, tributary (of imposts payable in money; whereas vectigalis denotes those payable in kind; the former was held to be the most humiliating; cf. ): civitas,; ; : Aedui,: oppidum,: provincia,: vectigal, i. e. a fixed yearly impost or contribution in money, : praedia,.—Plur. subst.: stī^pen-dĭārĭi, ōrum, m., tributaries (in money; whereas vectigales in kind): socii stipendiariique populi Romani,; ; ; ; (opp. vectigales) ; ; cf. ; fin.—Sing.: vectigalis stipendiariusque et servus populi Romani (Hannibal),.—
In milit. lang., receiving pay, serving for pay, stipendiary: (Romani) postquam stipendiarii facti sunt,: cohortes, Auct. B. Afr. 43.

la:verb:stillo.html:
stillo, āvi, ātum, 1, v. n. and
a [stilla].
Neutr., to drop, drip, trickle, distil (mostly poet.; syn. roro).
Lit.: vas, unde stillet lente aqua,: gutta (dulcedinis) in cor,: umorem, quasi igni cera super calido tabescens multa liquescat,: cruor ferro, (2, 8 b, 26 (10)): unguenta capillo,: de viridi ilice mella,: ros,: hammoniaci lacrima stillat m harenis,.—
Transf., of things which drop or drop with a liquid: saxa guttis manantibu' stillent,' paenula multo nimbo, : coma Syrio rore,: sanguine sidera,; cf.' arbor sanguineis roribus,; —Without abl.: umida saxa, super viridi stillantia musco, : ille, qui stillantem prae se pugionem tulit, * : uva,; .—
Trop.: stillantes voces,words that ooze out drop by drop,; cf.: orationem stillare,: plumis stillare diem,to be full, to abound in,.—
Act., to cause to drop, let fall in drops, to drop, distil: stillabit amicis Ex oculis rorem, * : coctam caepam cum adipe anserino,: stillata De ramis electra,dropped, distilled,: stillata cortice myrrha,; acre malum stillans ocellus,.—
Trop., to drop, instil: cum facilem stillavit in aurem Exiguum de veneno,.

la:verb:stipulor.gloss: to demand a formal promise, to bargain, to covenant, to stipulate
senses: to demand a formal promise, to bargain, to covenant, to stipulate
to promise, to engage, to pledge oneself
la:verb:stipulor.html:
stĭpŭlor, ātus, 1 (
inf. paragog. stipularier, ), v. dep.
acc. to Müll., kindr. with stips: qui pecuniam alligat, stipulari et restipulari; cf. also: cum spondetur pecunia, stipulari dicitur, Müll.—More prob. from unused adj. stipulus, firm, from root stip-; v. stipo
, jurid. t. t., to demand a formal promise; to bargain, covenant, stipulate.
